beats.intro: Module fourteen. [[sub]]Credit risk: what it is, how to measure it, and how it moves bond prices.
beats.cs: Analysts use the Cs of credit. [[b]]Five are specific to the borrower. [[c1]]Capacity, the ability to make payments. [[c2]]Capital, other resources that reduce reliance on debt. [[c3]]Collateral, the assets supporting the debt. [[c4]]Covenants, the legal terms. [[c5]]And character, management quality and willingness to pay. [[t]]Three are top-down, and affect all borrowers. [[c6]]Conditions, the economic and business environment. [[c7]]Country, its legal and political system. [[c8]]And currency, the effect of exchange rates.
beats.sources: Credit risk is the risk of loss when a borrower fails to pay in full and on time. [[corp]]A company repays mainly from its cash flow. Secured debt adds collateral as a second source. [[sov]]A sovereign repays from taxes and other government revenue, and, for foreign currency debt, from its ability to earn that currency. [[ill]]A borrower may be illiquid, unable to raise cash to pay now. That is different from insolvent, where assets are worth less than liabilities.
beats.el: Expected loss has two parts. [[pod]]The probability of default: the chance the issuer fails to pay. [[lgd]]And the loss given default: the exposure at default, times the share not recovered. [[f]]Expected loss is the probability of default, times the loss given default. [[ex]]Say the probability of default is five percent. The exposure is four hundred thousand euros, with one hundred thousand of collateral. So the claim at risk is three hundred thousand. With a recovery rate of ninety percent, the loss given default is thirty thousand. [[res]]Expected loss is five percent of thirty thousand: fifteen hundred euros.
beats.spread: Compare expected loss with the credit spread. [[f]]An investor is fairly compensated if the spread covers the expected loss. [[b]]BRWA's bond yields ninety basis points over Treasuries. With a one percent probability of default and an eighty percent loss given default, expected loss is eighty basis points. The spread is enough. [[v]]VIVU's bond yields four point two percent over Treasuries. A six percent probability of default and a fifty percent loss given default give three hundred basis points of expected loss. Again the spread covers it, with more risk, and more reward.
beats.drivers: What drives each part? [[pod]]The probability of default depends on profitability, coverage, and leverage. Higher margins, more earnings to cover interest, and less debt relative to earnings all mean lower default risk. [[lgd]]The loss given default depends on the claim's seniority and collateral. [[ig]]Investment grade investors worry most about a rising probability of default. [[hy]]High yield investors seek covenants and security, to reduce the loss given default.
beats.ratings: Credit ratings summarize default risk in symbols. [[ag]]Moody's, S&P, and Fitch assess issuers on a forward-looking basis. [[uses]]Ratings let investors compare issuers, trigger covenants and step-up coupons, and satisfy regulations. A fall to a lower rating is credit migration risk, or downgrade risk. [[pit]]But ratings have pitfalls. They lag market prices, since spreads change daily and ratings change rarely. They can overlook risks, as with subprime mortgage securities before the financial crisis. And the issuer pays for the rating. So investors should do their own analysis.
beats.cycle: Credit spreads move with the credit cycle. [[top]]They are narrowest near the top, when risk seems lowest. [[bot]]And widest near the bottom, when risk peaks. [[f]]The price effect of a spread change is minus modified duration times the spread change, plus half the convexity times the change squared. [[ex]]Take a high yield bond with modified duration four point five, and convexity twenty three. In a recession, spreads widen one hundred basis points. [[res]]The price falls about four point three nine percent.
beats.wrap: Let's recap. [[w1]]Expected loss is the probability of default times the loss given default. [[w2]]The credit spread should compensate for expected loss. [[w3]]Ratings help, but they lag, and can miss risks. [[w4]]Spreads widen in downturns, and the price effect follows duration and convexity.
